title: Alzheimer disease: tau (microtubule-associated protein) neurofibrillary tangles
vignette: A 74-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressive forgetfulness over the past 2 years. Her family states that the patient asks the same questions repeatedly over the course of a day and often forgets what she is doing in the middle of chores. The patient has also been more irritable but has had no movement or gait abnormalities, feelings of depression, hallucinations, or delusions. Medical conditions include hypertension and renal artery stenosis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Mini-Mental State Examination score is 21 out of 30 and she recalls 1 out of 3 objects after 5 minutes. There are no focal neurologic deficits. Which of the following is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

clues.text: progressive forgetfulness over the past 2 years
clues.note: Slowly progressive memory loss over years is the classic course of Alzheimer disease.

clues.text: no movement or gait abnormalities, feelings of depression, hallucinations, or delusions
clues.note: Absence of parkinsonism, visual hallucinations, or early psychiatric features argues against Lewy body dementia, vascular, or other dementias, favoring Alzheimer.

clues.text: recalls 1 out of 3 objects after 5 minutes
clues.note: Prominent impairment of recent (short-term) memory with otherwise nonfocal exam is characteristic of Alzheimer disease.

whatMatters: Progressive impairment of recent memory in an older adult without focal deficits, parkinsonism, or hallucinations = ALZHEIMER DISEASE. Its pathogenesis involves the microtubule-associated protein TAU, which becomes hyperphosphorylated and POLYMERIZES into intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (plus extracellular beta-amyloid plaques). Answer D (microtubule-associated protein polymerization).
strategy: Diagnose Alzheimer, then match the molecular lesion: hyperphosphorylated TAU (a microtubule-associated protein) forms paired helical filaments/neurofibrillary tangles; beta-amyloid forms extracellular plaques. Choose 'microtubule-associated protein polymerization' (tau). Reject alpha-synuclein (Lewy body dementia/Parkinson), CD4/myelin (multiple sclerosis), arteriolar vasculitis (CNS vasculitis), and perivascular virally infected macrophages (HIV dementia).

options.text: CD4+ T lymphocytes activated by myelin basic protein
Perivascular infiltration of virally infected macrophages

eliminations.label: Alpha-synuclein aggregation - Lewy body dementia/Parkinson (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: alpha-synuclein aggregates form Lewy bodies (dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those feature fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism - none present here; the amnestic, nonfocal picture fits Alzheimer (tau/amyloid). ✅ Correct if: fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism.

eliminations.label: CD4/myelin basic protein - multiple sclerosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: autoimmune CD4 T-cell attack on CNS myelin = multiple sclerosis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: MS affects young adults with focal deficits disseminated in time/space, not an elderly amnestic dementia. ✅ Correct if: young adult with relapsing focal neurologic deficits.

eliminations.label: Arteriolar vasculitis - CNS vasculitis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: inflammatory vasculitis of cerebral arterioles. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: CNS vasculitis usually causes headache and focal deficits from ischemia, not a slowly progressive amnestic dementia. ✅ Correct if: headache + focal strokes with vessel inflammation.

eliminations.label: Perivascular virally infected macrophages - HIV dementia
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: HIV-associated dementia (microglial nodules/multinucleated giant cells from infected macrophages). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it occurs in advanced HIV as a subcortical dementia, not this cortical amnestic picture in an immunocompetent elder. ✅ Correct if: advanced HIV with subcortical cognitive decline.

reasoning: Progressive recent-memory loss in an older adult without focal deficits/parkinsonism/hallucinations = Alzheimer disease
Alzheimer neuropathology: extracellular beta-amyloid plaques + intracellular neurofibrillary tangles
Tangles form when the microtubule-associated protein TAU is hyperphosphorylated and polymerizes
mechanism: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia, presenting with insidious, progressive impairment of RECENT memory and other cognitive domains, typically without early focal neurologic signs or movement disorder. Two hallmark neuropathologic lesions develop: (1) extracellular BETA-AMYLOID PLAQUES from aggregation of amyloid-beta (cleaved from amyloid precursor protein), and (2) intracellular NEUROFIBRILLARY TANGLES made of TAU. TAU is a MICROTUBULE-ASSOCIATED PROTEIN that normally stabilizes neuronal microtubules; in Alzheimer disease it becomes HYPERPHOSPHORYLATED, dissociates from microtubules (disrupting axonal transport), and POLYMERIZES into paired helical filaments that accumulate as tangles, driving neuronal dysfunction and death with resulting cortical atrophy. Thus the pathogenic process among the options is microtubule-associated (tau) protein polymerization. The distractors are mechanisms of other diseases: alpha-synuclein (Lewy body dementia/Parkinson), CD4/myelin basic protein (multiple sclerosis), arteriolar vasculitis (CNS vasculitis), and perivascular infected macrophages (HIV-associated dementia).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > Alzheimer disease: extracellular beta-amyloid plaques + intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau, a microtubule-associated protein); cortical atrophy; recent-memory loss.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Amnestic dementia without focal signs = Alzheimer; the tangle protein is tau (microtubule-associated), which polymerizes.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on tau/microtubule-associated protein, neurofibrillary tangles, beta-amyloid, or Lewy body/alpha-synuclein? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Alpha-synuclein = Lewy body/Parkinson; CD4/myelin = MS; arteriolar vasculitis = CNS vasculitis; infected macrophages = HIV dementia.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: Alzheimer = amyloid plaques (extracellular) + tau tangles (intracellular, hyperphosphorylated microtubule-associated protein).

keywords.front: Progressive recent-memory dementia, no focal signs

keywords.back: Detaches from microtubules -> disrupts axonal transport, forms tangles

firstAid.detail: Neuro: tau (microtubule-associated) hyperphosphorylation -> neurofibrillary tangles; + beta-amyloid plaques.
Neuro > alpha-synuclein (Lewy), CD4/myelin (MS), vasculitis, HIV macrophages.
Neuro > extracellular amyloid plaques + intracellular tau tangles; cortical atrophy.

memoryHook: Alzheimer's tau lets go of the microtubule scaffolding and clumps into tangles - a normally helpful railroad protein derailing memory.
